title: Berakhot opens at bedtime
hookLine: this block reads Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, from beginning to end
carry: a tractate is woven: read it in order
tomorrow: the night has watches. who's awake in them?

cards: A box set of a show you've never watched, dozens of episodes, and a friend says: start at the beginning, no skipping. A tractate of Talmud asks the same thing.
This block reads one, Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, from its first page to its last. Slowly, a little each day, the way a long show gets watched. And its first page is numbered two.

teach.b: The word is masechet, a tractate: one book of the Talmud, on one subject.
The same Hebrew word names the woven web in the story of Samson, cloth on a loom, and some readers hear that in it: a tractate is woven, threads of voices crossing.
Pick up a printed volume and your senses tell you the rest.
It's heavy. It smells like old paper. On each page, a block of text sits in the middle, the Mishnah and its discussion, with smaller commentaries wrapped around it.
And it opens on page two, side a.
Berakhot's first question isn't about God or belief. It's about the clock. From when do we recite the Shema in the evening?
The Mishnah answers: from the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion, until the end of the first watch, says Rabbi Eliezer. The sages say, until midnight. Rabban Gamaliel says, until dawn.
Three answers on the first page, and nobody is erased. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: Berakhot opens with an argument about bedtime. That's why this block reads in order.
Skip around and you collect quotes.

teach.h: A TRACTATE IS WOVEN: READ IT IN ORDER.
teach.b: Read one tractate start to finish and you hear a conversation: threads coming back, names you'll meet again. Berakhot is about blessings, the Shema, prayer, words over food, and for the next weeks it's ours, page by page.

how: Many Jews learn Talmud a page at a time, in order, often with a study partner or in a daily class; finishing a whole tractate is marked with a siyum, a small celebration.

practice: Find something woven near you: a sleeve, a scarf, a towel, the spine of a book. Run a fingertip slowly along it and feel where the threads cross.
Let that be the picture for the sit: many threads, one piece, held together by going in order.
